records.concept: Increasingly, homeowners are opting to place wood-burning inserts into masonry fireplaces; many manufacturers of wood-burning stoves produce inserts that fit directly into the firebox and make use of existing chimneys, creating a more efficient heat source for the dwelling.
records.rule_plain_language: A wood-burning insert drops into an existing firebox and uses the existing chimney.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: A renovation strategy that keeps the existing fireplace footprint unchanged.

evidence.source_anchor: inserts that fit directly into the firebox
evidence.source_anchor_description: Closing paragraph on wood-burning inserts.
evidence.supports: Inserts fit the existing firebox and reuse the existing chimney.

records.concept: Wood-burning fireplaces may be illegal in some localities and in some locations there may be burn bans for certain periods of time based on air pollution levels; there are regional differences in masonry fireplace construction, and finding a highly skilled mason with a good track record is the key to a successful masonry fireplace.
records.condition: Depends on local jurisdiction and air pollution regulation.
records.rule_plain_language: Wood-burning fireplaces are not permitted everywhere; local rules and regional practice govern.

evidence.source_anchor: may be illegal in some localities
evidence.source_anchor_description: Fifth and sixth bullets of the Additional Fireplace Notes box.
evidence.supports: Local legality, burn bans and regional construction differences.

records.concept: The size of the fireplace opening and surrounding masonry mass is highly variable; this must be scaled for the space it is within, as well as for how much heat it is intended to produce; it has been said that the least efficient way to heat your home is with an open fireplace, and glass enclosures or inserts increase efficiency.
records.rule_plain_language: Scale the fireplace to its room; there is no single correct size.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Supports proportional rather than fixed sizing of a fireplace when generating a room; no ratio is given.

evidence.source_anchor: must be scaled for the space it is within
evidence.source_anchor_description: First and fourth bullets of the Additional Fireplace Notes box.
evidence.supports: Scaling of opening and mass to the room and the intended heat output.

measurements.relationship_expression: fireplace opening and mass scale with room size and intended heat output

records.concept: Configuration a: a one-side-open masonry fireplace in an exterior frame wall; this inside-outside type of fireplace produces very little net heat gain because a great deal is lost by conduction and radiation directly to the exterior.
records.rule_plain_language: A fireplace set into an exterior wall loses most of its heat outside.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item a of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Placement in an exterior wall and its poor net heat gain.

records.concept: Configuration b: a one-side-open masonry fireplace against an exterior or interior wall; this configuration will lose less heat to the exterior than type a.
records.rule_plain_language: Standing the fireplace against the wall instead of inside it keeps more heat in the room.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item b of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Fireplace standing against a wall loses less heat than one set into the wall.

records.concept: Configuration c: a one-side-open masonry fireplace set at a 45-degree angle into a corner works well in certain spaces; this configuration has a loss of heat similar to type b.
records.rule_plain_language: A corner fireplace sits at 45 degrees across the corner.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Gives the standard rotation for a corner fireplace when generating a layout.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item c of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: 45-degree corner placement and its heat behaviour.

records.concept: Configuration d: a one-side-open freestanding masonry fireplace radiates heat to all directions of the interior space; this type can be used as a room divider.
records.rule_plain_language: A freestanding fireplace heats in every direction and can act as a divider between zones.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Directly relevant to zoning: a freestanding fireplace is a legitimate separator between two functional zones.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item d of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Freestanding fireplace radiates in all directions and can divide a room.

records.concept: Configuration e: a two-side-open freestanding masonry fireplace disperses radiant heat similarly to type d; it is preferable to have glass in the fireplace opening on both sides, with one side fixed and the other operable, as a means of building and tending the fire; without the glass this type is very vulnerable to allowing smoke into the rooms with the least cross-draft.
records.rule_plain_language: A double-sided freestanding fireplace should have glass on both sides, one fixed and one operable.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item e of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Two-side-open behaviour, glass recommendation and smoke risk.

records.concept: Configuration f: a two-side-open masonry fireplace can work in a corner with either closed side against a wall, or freestanding; without a glass enclosure this type is prone to the smoking problem described in type e.
records.rule_plain_language: A two-sided fireplace can sit in a corner with one closed side to a wall, or stand free.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item f of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Corner or freestanding placement of a two-side-open fireplace and its smoke risk.

records.concept: Configuration g: a three-side-open masonry fireplace requires a large masonry mass if it is necessary to cantilever a masonry hood over the firebox; this type is very prone to smoking if there is no glass enclosure.
records.rule_plain_language: A three-sided fireplace needs a big masonry mass to carry the hood and smokes easily without glass.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item g of Figure 9-10.
evidence.supports: Structural and smoke consequences of a three-side-open fireplace.

records.concept: Configuration h: an open fire pit with a hood, generally made of sheet metal, is not recommended for indoor residential applications and is very prone to smoke drifting horizontally into adjacent interior space; even this type requires a firebrick floor.
records.rule_plain_language: Hooded open fire pits are not recommended inside a house.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: A clear negative rule candidate: do not place an open hooded fire pit in an interior residential space.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item h of Figure 9-10 and the notes beneath the legend.
evidence.supports: Fire pit unsuitable indoors; horizontal smoke drift; firebrick floor still required.

records.concept: Exposed surfaces of these fireplaces are made of brick, stone, or ceramic; sheet metal hoods are often used in types f and g.
records.rule_plain_language: Fireplace surfaces are brick, stone or ceramic; hoods are sheet metal.
records.possible_remlab_interpretation: Defines the plausible visible finish materials of a fireplace surround in a render.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Notes beneath the Figure 9-10 legend.
evidence.supports: Exposed surface materials and use of sheet metal hoods.

records.concept: A round flue is shown in the configuration drawings; this is required by some codes, and square or rectangular flues may be allowed.
records.condition: Depends on the applicable local code.
records.rule_plain_language: Round flues are preferred and sometimes required; square or rectangular ones may be permitted.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Notes beneath the Figure 9-10 legend.
evidence.supports: Round flue required by some codes; other shapes may be allowed.

evidence.source_anchor_description: Legend item I of Figure 9-7b (a round flue is best).
evidence.supports: Round cross section preferred for the flue.

top_findings.why_useful: Fireplace placement must enhance the room without impeding traffic flow or making the room difficult to furnish - a direct scoring criterion for generated layouts.
Central door placement divides a room in half while corner placement pushes circulation to the edges and frees the interior for furniture groups.
Window placement should support multiple furniture layouts rather than a single one - directly applicable to layout generation and evaluation.
Floor material transitions belong directly under the closed door leaf - an unambiguous geometric rule for finish boundaries.
Door swings should land against a blank wall and must not overlap circulation or other swings - a checkable opening-envelope constraint.
